summary: This memo describes the US top-level domains on the Internet, replacing RFC 1386. It explains how names under .us are organised by geography.

eli5.summary: Every country gets its own ending for web names. This paper explains how the United States organised names ending in .us.

questions: how is the us domain organized
how are us domain names structured
what is k12 in a us domain name
how do i delegate a us domain subdomain
subtitle: How the .us domain is organized by state and locality, and how names are registered and delegated under it.

tldr.problem: Organizations in the United States had mostly registered under EDU and COM, and the .us country domain needed a clear structure for names, schools and delegation.
tldr.mechanism: Names under .us follow political geography: state code, then locality or a special branch such as K12, CC, LIB, STATE, FED, DNI or GEN. Registration is direct or by delegating a branch to an administrator who runs at least two name servers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1480 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1386 and records the rules of the US Domain in mid-1993.

facts.label: Hierarchy
facts.value: State, then locality or special branch

facts.label: Registration turnaround
facts.value: A few days; name servers updated 12 to 24 hours later

today: RFC 1480 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1386, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting it. It describes the US Domain rules as of June 1993.

sections.title: Introduction to the US Domain
sections.content:
The memo starts with a short tour of the Domain Name System (DNS), which translates hostnames such as venera.isi.edu to IP addresses. It was created because the old single HOSTS.TXT file kept by the InterNIC no longer scaled, and organizations wanted to manage their own names.

The top-level domains were EDU, COM, GOV, MIL, ORG, INT, NET and the two-letter ISO-3166 country codes. US is the code for the United States, so the US Domain is an official top-level domain. In practice most US organizations had registered under EDU and COM, so little use was made of it at first. The domain administrators were Jon Postel and Ann Westine Cooper at USC-ISI. Any computer in the United States may be registered in it.
sections.eli5: DNS is the Internet's phone book that turns names into numbers. Every country gets its own section, and .us is the section for the United States.

sections.title: The Naming Structure
sections.content:
The US Domain hierarchy follows political geography: state, then locality (a city or county), then organization or computer. Examples are BERKELEY.CA.US and PORTLAND.WA.US. State codes are the two-letter US Postal abbreviations. The things being named are individual computers.

Several special branches exist. Parallel to the states are FED for federal agencies and DNI for distributed national institutes that span states. Within a state are CI and CO for city and county government, K12 for public school districts (with a pseudo district PVT for private schools), CC for community colleges, TEC for technical and vocational schools, LIB for libraries, STATE for state agencies and GEN for things that fit nowhere else, such as clubs and domain parks. Businesses register directly under their locality, for example Zuckys.Santa-Monica.CA.US.

The organizational names EDU, COM and so on are deliberately not used inside the US Domain, to avoid confusion. The authors also argue that structure and longer names let more people get their obviously right name.
sections.eli5: It works like a street address: country, state, town, then the building. School names like Washington High are common, so adding the district and state tells them apart.

sections.title: Schools and Other Special Branches
sections.content:
Schools get detailed treatment. There are many Washington high schools but only one can be Washington.EDU, and dumping every school into EDU would make that zone unmanageably large. So K12 schools register as <school>.<district>.K12.<state>.US, for example Hamilton.LA-Unified.K12.CA.US. Where needed, the words Elementary, Middle and High distinguish schools with the same name.

Private schools may register like businesses under a locality, or under the artificial district PVT, such as Crossroads.PVT.K12.CA.US. The reason for PVT is delegation: a district administrator may later run the district branch, and a private school should not depend on that person. Special schools and service units can go under a pseudo district or directly under K12.
sections.eli5: Many towns have a school with the same name. Putting the district and state in the name is like adding your last name and city so people know which Sam you mean.

sections.title: Registration and Delegation
sections.content:
There are two kinds of registration: delegation, where a branch is handed to an organization running name servers, and direct registration, where information goes straight into the main database. Anyone registering fills out a US Domain template requested from us-domain@isi.edu. Both an administrator and a technical contact with working mailboxes must be given. If everything checks out, registering a host usually takes a few days, and name servers are updated 12 to 24 hours later.

Hosts without IP addresses, for example UUCP hosts, may register if an Internet forwarder host agrees to relay their mail, with an MX record pointing to it. Delegation requires a knowledgeable technical contact, at least two independent name servers in physically separate locations, equal treatment of all applicants, timely processing, and notice to the US Domain Administrator of changes.

Delegation of a whole state name space was not yet implemented. Locality administrators register businesses directly and handle the CI and CO branches, and K12 administrators are responsible for the PVT pseudo district.
sections.eli5: You fill in a form and name a grown-up contact. Big groups can run their own part of the phone book, but they need two helpers in different places in case one has a power cut.

sections.title: Database Information and Wildcards
sections.content:
The DNS database is divided into zones held by name servers, and every zone must be available on at least two servers. The memo lists seven name servers then supporting the US Domain, including venera.isi.edu and ns.uu.net. Records in zone files are resource records of the form <name> [<ttl>] [<class>] <type> <data>. Common types are SOA, NS, A, CNAME, HINFO, WKS, MX and PTR. A CNAME can point an old name to a new one if an organization moves.

The memo also covers wildcard records of the form *.<anydomain>. They apply to descendants of the domain but not to the domain itself. The authors believe each host should be explicitly registered, because wildcards hide the hosts under a subdomain, yet they allow wildcards under organizational subdomains such as *.DWP.LA.CA.US, and not under a city or state domain.
sections.eli5: The phone book is cut into chapters, and each chapter is kept in at least two places. A wildcard is a note saying: any name in this chapter, send the mail to this one mailroom.
